related_questions.snippet: The overall goals of antiepileptic therapy are to prevent seizures and avoid untoward side effects with a regimen that is convenient and easy to follow. People with epilepsy usually initiate treatment with one antiepileptic drug at the time of diagnosis, but 30 percent of patients will be refractory to this medication.

related_questions.question: What do antiepileptic drugs do to the brain?
related_questions.snippet: Antiepileptic drugs (AEDs) can adversely affect cognitive function by suppressing neuronal excitability or enhancing inhibitory neurotransmission. The main cognitive effects of AEDs are impaired attention, vigilance, and psychomotor speed, but secondary effects can manifest on other cognitive functions.

text_blocks.snippet: Antiepileptic medications, also known as antiepileptic drugs (AEDs) or anticonvulsants, are used to treat epilepsy and other seizure disorders by reducing the frequency and/or severity of seizures. These medications work by affecting the electrical activity in the brain to prevent or stop seizures. Commonly prescribed AEDs include lamotrigine, levetiracetam, carbamazepine, phenytoin, topiramate, and gabapentin.
snippet_highlighted_words: used to treat epilepsy and other seizure disorders by reducing the frequency and/or severity of seizures

list.snippet: Prevent seizures: AEDs help regulate brain activity to reduce the likelihood of seizures.
Control seizures: They can also reduce the severity or duration of seizures that do occur.
Treat epilepsy and other seizure disorders: This includes both generalized and focal seizures.
May be used for other conditions: AEDs can also be prescribed for neuropathic pain, bipolar disorder, and other conditions, according to the Mayo Clinic.

list.title: Broad-spectrum AEDs:
list.snippet: Effective for a wide range of seizure types. Examples include lamotrigine, levetiracetam, topiramate, and zonisamide.

list.title: Narrow-spectrum AEDs:
list.snippet: Primarily used for focal seizures. Examples include ethosuximide, pregabalin, gabapentin, and carbamazepine.
Lamotrigine (Lamictal): Effective for both focal and generalized seizures.
Levetiracetam (Keppra): Effective for focal and generalized seizures, may worsen myoclonic seizures.
Carbamazepine (Tegretol): Effective for focal and generalized tonic-clonic seizures.
Phenytoin (Dilantin): Used for various seizure types.
Topiramate (Topamax): Effective for focal and generalized seizures.
Gabapentin (Neurontin): Effective for focal seizures, may be used for neuropathic pain.

list.title: Individualized treatment:
list.snippet: The best AED for a person depends on the specific type of seizures, individual characteristics, and potential side effects.

list.title: Side effects:
list.snippet: AEDs can cause side effects, and it's important to discuss any concerns with a healthcare professional.

list.title: Drug interactions:
list.snippet: Some AEDs can interact with other medications, so it's crucial to inform the doctor about all medications being taken.

list.title: Emergency treatment:
list.snippet: Some AEDs are used for emergency treatment of status epilepticus (prolonged seizures).

list.title: Consult a neurologist:
list.snippet: A neurologist can properly diagnose the type of seizure disorder and recommend the most appropriate AED.

list.title: Follow the doctor's instructions:
list.snippet: It's crucial to take AEDs as prescribed and not to stop taking them without consulting the doctor.
